chapter_title: Automated Checks, Cost, and Student Privacy
learning_objective: The learner will judge whether each of ten items is safe to send to an AI service, needs approval or anonymizing first, or must not be sent, with at least 9 of 10 correct on the first attempt.
specification:
Type: microsim **sim-id:** student-data-sorter
**Library:** p5.js
**Status:** Specified
**Bloom Level:** Evaluate
**Bloom Verb:** judge
**Learning Objective:** The learner will judge whether each of ten items is safe to send to an AI service, needs approval or anonymizing first, or must not be sent, with at least 9 of 10 correct on the first attempt. **Prerequisites:** Student Data Privacy, FERPA, AI Assistant (defined in Chapter 12) (all defined in this chapter above this block or in Chapter 12). **Evidence of Mastery:** For each item the learner commits one of three bins. A placement is correct when it matches the Correct bin column in Content. Mastery is at least 9 of 10 correct on the first attempt. Reading the definitions is exploration, not evidence. **Misconceptions:** (1) Removing names always makes data anonymous. (2) A small class cannot be identified from its scores. (3) Anything a teacher already holds is safe to send. **Instructional Rationale:** Judging whether an item may be sent is an Evaluate-level action that applies a privacy rule. Ten items that include re-identifiable ones teach the learner that anonymizing takes more than deleting names. **Content:** The three bins: Safe to send (public material with no student data), Needs approval or anonymizing first (could identify students, or is sensitive), and Do not send (clearly identifies a student or is private). The ten items: | # | Item shown to the learner | Correct bin | Why (shown as feedback) | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | The published text of an open textbook chapter. | Safe to send | It is public and holds no student data. | | 2 | A rubric prompt template with placeholders. | Safe to send | It holds no student data. | | 3 | A class's quiz scores listed with student names. | Needs approval or anonymizing first | The names make the scores personal data. | | 4 | A spreadsheet of grades with student ID numbers. | Do not send | It is identifiable and sensitive. | | 5 | A photograph of a student. | Do not send | It identifies a person. | | 6 | Quiz results with names replaced by codes, from a class of four students. | Needs approval or anonymizing first | In a very small group, the scores may still identify students. | | 7 | A teacher's own lesson plan with no student information. | Safe to send | It holds no student data. | | 8 | An email thread with a parent about a student's progress. | Do not send | It is private and identifies a student. | | 9 | A public district policy document. | Safe to send | It is public and holds no student data. | | 10 | Unsigned survey comments from a class of 120 students. | Needs approval or anonymizing first | Comments can reveal who wrote them, so check them before sending. | **Provenance:** The items are illustrative cases written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The sim states that it is a study aid and not legal advice, and that a school's own policy decides. **Rules:** Each item has exactly one correct bin. Four items are Safe to send, three are Needs approval or anonymizing first, and three are Do not send. **Learner Activity:** 1. The learner sees one item and the three bins. 2. The learner places the item in a bin, and the placement is committed. 3. The sim shows whether it was correct and the Why text. 4. After item 10 the sim shows the summary. **Feedback:** 10 items in a shuffled order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [bin]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. This is [bin]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 10 correct on the first attempt". At 9 or more it adds "You can keep student data out of an AI service." Below 9 it lists the Why text of each missed item. **Starting State:** The first item and the three bins. The question shown is "May this go to an AI service?" **Chapter Anchors:** The chapter's worked example sorts a public textbook chapter and a rubric prompt as safe, class scores with names as needing anonymizing first, and a grade spreadsheet, a photograph, and a parent email as not to be sent.
